leftEvidence.title: A silent sheep text becomes good news about Jesus

points.label: Action and sequence
points.left: An Ethiopian official reads Isaiah’s silent sheep passage and asks whom it concerns; Philip begins from that Scripture and announces the good news about Jesus.
points.right: A communal “we,” the servant, the LORD, oppressors, and later offspring appear without collapsing into one voice.

points.label: Evidence boundary
points.left: This later passage uses Crucifixion language inside its own argument without retelling the complete Gospel event.
points.right: The servant is acted upon and also described as acting, while the passage attributes outcomes to the LORD.

payload.posture: Acts explicitly begins good news about Jesus from a bounded reading of Isaiah’s silent-sheep language.

rightEvidence.title: The servant rejected, wounded, silent, and allotted a portion

payload.tension: Isaiah preserves an extended servant poem; Acts preserves a reader’s question and an apostolic interpretation without reproducing the whole source.
payload.title: Silent sheep read / servant passage heard
